sections.title: Loft conversion type
sections.helper: The conversion type is the biggest cost driver. Choose what suits your roof structure and budget.

options.label: Velux / Rooflight conversion
options.desc: No change to the roofline. Velux or rooflight windows inserted between existing rafters. Lowest cost option. Needs roof pitch of 40°+ and adequate head height (2.2m+ at ridge).

options.label: Rear dormer (standard)
options.desc: A flat-roofed box structure projecting from the rear slope. The most common London loft conversion. Creates a vertical front face with windows, dramatically increasing usable headroom.

options.label: Full-width rear dormer
options.desc: Dormer runs the full width of the rear slope from party wall to party wall. Maximum space. Popular in wider London terraces and semis.

options.label: Hip-to-gable + rear dormer
options.desc: The sloping hip-end of the roof is converted to a vertical gable wall, combined with a rear dormer. Maximises floor area. Most common on 1930s/1950s semis and detached houses.

options.label: L-shaped dormer (rear + back-addition)
options.desc: A dormer on the main rear slope combined with a dormer over the back-addition / return of a Victorian or Edwardian terraced house. Creates L-shaped floor plan — often two bedrooms + bathroom.

options.label: Mansard conversion
options.desc: The entire rear roof slope is rebuilt at a near-vertical angle (72°) topped by a shallow flat roof. Maximum space gain — often creates a full floor. Almost always requires planning permission. Premium option.

sections.title: Existing roof structure
sections.helper: The type of existing roof structure significantly affects how much work is needed to create a habitable space.

options.label: Traditional cut rafter (Victorian / Edwardian / 1930s)
options.desc: Individual rafters and purlins. Open roof space — easiest to convert. No web members to remove. Standard starting point for loft conversions.

options.label: Trussed rafter roof (post-1960s, modern)
options.desc: Factory-made triangular trusses. Very common in 1960s–1990s houses. The W-shaped web members must be entirely removed and replaced with a new structural frame. Adds significant cost.

options.label: Flat or low-pitch roof (unusual configuration)
options.desc: Unusual situation — flat or near-flat roof above, or complex multi-pitch configuration. Requires detailed survey before works. Higher design and structural cost.

sections.title: Existing head height at ridge
sections.helper: Building Regulations require a minimum of 2.2m head height over at least 50% of the floor area for a habitable room.

options.label: Good (2.5m+ at ridge)
options.desc: Plenty of headroom. Full habitable space achievable without structural alterations to roof height.

options.label: Borderline (2.2–2.5m at ridge)
options.desc: Achievable with good design. May limit usable floor area slightly or require lower floor build-up. Dormer becomes more valuable for headroom.

options.label: Limited (under 2.2m at ridge)
options.desc: May require ridge raising, floor lowering into ceiling below, or may not be viable without major structural work. Requires structural engineer assessment.

sections.title: Staircase
sections.helper: A new staircase is always required. The type affects cost, space used, and look. Fire regs require FD30 fire doors on all floors.

options.label: Space-saving / alternating tread
options.desc: Steeper stair with alternating foot treads. Where space is very tight. Meets Building Regs for loft access. Most compact option.

options.label: Standard winder (quarter-turn, softwood)
options.desc: Standard softwood winder staircase. Space-efficient. Most common choice for loft conversions. Balustrading included.

options.label: Hardwood straight flight
options.desc: Solid oak or ash treads and handrail. Straight flight (requires more landing space). Higher aesthetic quality.

options.label: Bespoke / glass / floating steel
options.desc: Architectural staircase — floating treads, glass balustrade, structural steel spine. Feature piece. High fabrication and install time.

sections.title: En-suite bathroom
sections.helper: An en-suite is one of the biggest value-adds of a loft conversion. Plumbing must be run up from the floor below.

options.label: No en-suite
options.desc: Bedroom only. Residents use existing bathroom on floor below. No new plumbing required.

options.label: Basic en-suite (shower, WC, basin)
options.desc: Compact but complete. Standard sanitaryware. Walk-in shower enclosure, close-coupled WC, pedestal basin. Tiled wet area.

options.label: Mid-range en-suite
options.desc: Better quality suite and tiling. Concealed shower valve, wall-hung WC, vanity unit. More tile coverage.

options.label: High-spec en-suite
options.desc: Walk-in wetroom shower, freestanding / wall-hung fixtures, large format tiles, full room tiling, heated towel rail, premium sanitaryware.

sections.title: Dormer cladding
sections.helper: Applies if you have a dormer, hip-to-gable, L-shaped, or mansard conversion. Affects aesthetics and cost.

options.label: Render (monocouche / through-colour)
options.desc: Standard and affordable. Smooth or textured render finish. Easy to repaint. Common choice across London.

options.label: Slate tile hanging
options.desc: Vertical slate tiles on dormer face. Traditional and durable. Matches many Victorian and Edwardian properties. Lifetime of 50+ years.

options.label: Zinc standing seam
options.desc: Premium contemporary finish. Standing seam zinc panels. Very popular in London for a clean, modern look. Low maintenance, very long lifespan.

options.label: Timber (cedar / larch)
options.desc: Natural timber cladding. Cedar weathers to silver-grey. Warm aesthetic. Requires maintenance or treatment every 5–10 years.

sections.title: Windows & rooflights
sections.helper: Light is critical in loft conversions. Standard Velux rooflights vs larger feature windows vs a Juliet balcony.

options.label: Velux rooflights only (2–3 units)
options.desc: Standard Velux or similar pitched-roof windows. Sufficient for Velux conversion. Also used alongside dormer windows.

options.label: Velux + standard dormer windows
options.desc: Rooflights combined with standard-sized windows in dormer face (uPVC or aluminium casement).

options.label: Large aluminium dormer windows
options.desc: Oversized aluminium casement or fixed windows on dormer face. Maximises natural light. Slim frames. More glass area.

options.label: Juliet balcony (glass balustrade)
options.desc: Full-height glass door with structural glass balustrade. No floor area gain but maximises light and views. Popular feature on rear dormers.

sections.title: Electrics
sections.helper: Building Regs require mains-wired, interlinked smoke alarms on all floors including the loft.

options.label: Basic (standard lighting, sockets, linked smoke alarms)
options.desc: Ceiling pendant, sockets, switches, mains-linked smoke detectors. Meets Building Regs. First and second fix included.

options.label: Standard upgrade (recessed spots, mirror light, shaver point)
options.desc: Recessed LED downlights, bedside sockets, mirror/vanity light, USB charging sockets, shaver point.

options.label: Full feature electrics (LED niches, dimmers, sensors)
options.desc: Feature LED niches, dimmer circuits, motion sensors, TV point, data point, upgraded consumer unit contribution. Higher design and install time.

sections.title: Party wall
sections.helper: Nearly all London terraced and semi-detached loft conversions trigger Party Wall Act obligations. Notices must be served before work starts.

options.label: No party wall (detached house)
options.desc: No shared walls. No Party Wall Act obligations.

options.label: One adjoining owner (semi-detached)
options.desc: Notice to one neighbour. If they dissent, award needed. Surveyor fees: £1,000–£4,000 per side.

options.label: Two adjoining owners (terraced)
options.desc: Notices to both neighbours. Two sets of potential surveyor fees. Very common for London Victorian terraces.

sections.title: Planning permission
sections.helper: Most rear dormers are permitted development. Mansards and front dormers almost always need planning. Conservation areas remove PD rights.

options.label: Permitted development (no planning needed)
options.desc: Volume added ≤40m³ (terraced) or ≤50m³ (semi/detached). Rear slope only. Not in conservation area. Building Regs always required regardless.

options.label: Planning permission required
options.desc: Conservation area / front dormer / mansard / volume exceeded / Article 4 Direction. Includes application fee (£528), architect's planning drawings, 8-week determination period.

sections.title: Professional fees
sections.helper: Structural engineer is always needed. Architect drawings are needed for Building Regs. Party wall surveyor if applicable.

options.label: Not included (arrange separately)
options.desc: Handle architect and structural engineer independently. Typical range: £2,500–£8,000 for standard loft.

options.label: Architect + structural engineer
options.desc: Building regs drawings and SE calculations. The minimum required package for a loft conversion. SE full package typically £1,500–£4,000.

options.label: Full service (architect + SE + project management)
options.desc: Complete professional package from design through to snagging and sign-off. Includes planning application if required.

sections.title: Finish level
sections.helper: Applied as a multiplier across the whole project. Covers materials, fixtures, fittings, and detailing quality.

options.label: Standard
options.desc: Good quality practical finish. Standard materials throughout. Clean, tidy, habitable result. No frills.

options.label: Mid-range
options.desc: Better materials, upgraded fixtures, more detailing time. The most popular finish level in London.

options.label: Premium
options.desc: High-end materials, designer fixtures, precision detailing, longer labour time. Matching premium London standard.
